title: reality check
pros:
here’s the reality as i see it.

we all know the utility industry is changing both because of regulations and technology. 

executive management know change is coming but not exactly how is will impact the business. in times of doubt you make changes to show that you are at least aware something needs to be done. the easiest was to do this is through visible right-sizing of staff and implementing corporate change initiatives such as diversity and community service.

this is neither good nor bad, just reality in a semi-regulated industry. 

one thing is certain, the software, processes and procedures supporting the business all need to simplify. alliant energy is not so unique that it needs to have support systems that have been customized so extensively. 

as these customizations are removed the need for internal support is naturally going to decrease with a rippling affect. support will be outsourced to vendors who also service other companies with the same software and processes. from a business stand point this takes away the complicated tasks of hardware maintenance, upgrades, backups, disaster recovery and audits while also mitigating security risks.

i say if you are offered a job at alliant you go in knowing that you are part of the current plan for the future and should be ok for 3-5 years. just look out for the big leaps in change in the industry and have a plan b.

if you are currently employed at alliant take an honest look at what you and your supervisor do and determine if it is overly complicated or is done just because it has always been done that way. if so, try to keep a positive attitude and have an out strategy ready.

title: worth reading - good technical capabilities but frequent management changes
pros: great team of peers and extended team of subject matter experts (i worked in environment, health and safety). excellent cooperation from functional organizations and operational leadership and staff. i believe this is a good starter company for someone who is early in their career or mid-career and looking to make a change, but long-term career prospects may be challenging (see 'cons'). for anyone considering westinghouse, i recommend having a career plan that includes an ongoing job search and trigger points about when to bail.
cons: frequent management changes (3 ceo's, 6 executive vp's in my quality/ehs department, 6 directors and 3 managers in 6-1/2 years). when management changes, everything changes and many ongoing initiatives get delayed or dropped, so there is often a feeling of frustration because of wasted time and effort, or because of dropping an initiative under one leader only to resume it again later under another (we never deleted any past work - kept it handy!). also, and especially with the 2-year covid shut down, there seemed to be a lot of urgent but unimportant administrative work, or project rework that took up way too much of our time (many 60 to 70-hour weeks on salary). the company talks a lot about servant leadership but its culture is very conservative, risk-averse, and in practice, leadership has a very structured top-down approach. there is little or no opportunity to initiate positive change from non-leader-coded positions, and even then, typically only director and above have a voice. many functional, administrative and even some engineering positions are being eliminated or are required to 're-bid' for their jobs, and westinghouse is currently owned by an asset management company, so future dramatic changes may be on the horizon. wec has a career / professional development program but it has little depth for individual contributors or managers below director level, and in practice, career or professional development expenses are often cut out of departmental budgets. wec is a federal contractor so covid vaccines are required unless they grant a religious or medical accommodation. i do not have information on how disposed their leadership is to these accommodations, because i was laid off while i was seeking a religious accommodation. i can say with certainty that the internal communications regarding vaccinations got progressively less courteous and more dictatorial over the last half of 2021.

title: a company with one fatal flaw
pros:
the environment is quite lax when you walk around the call center, even before covid struck our nation. people are, for the most part, friendly, and during my tenure there it was very easy to talk to them in order to resolve their issues. of course, there were problematic people, but for every one of those you have a dozen others who are willing to work with you in a more concise fashion.

for note: mental illness is not equivalent to physical. and it felt as if the management in charge of my department had been constantly looking for ways to get me out of the company simply because i had a disability. 

if you have a mental disability, it might make your stay here an uphill battle. if you can push through it, the benefits are incredible, but tread carefully.

- only chemical engineering degrees are truly valued in the company. this is a not-so-secret expectation on how to quickly accelerate your career here.
- sustainability initiatives are minimal
- in order to be successful, you are required to follow a traditional career path through manufacturing roles
- if you do something bad, supervisors will not support you. if you do something good, supervisors will take credit for the work you did. 
- the expectation is that you need to respond within 24 hours if someone needs you while on vacation
- the cultural issues stem throughout the entire company! not only within one function (i.e. chemicals vs. upstream or supply chain vs. technical)
- a supervisor once told me "the people who do well here take ownership," which is ironic considering that the company as a whole has not been taking ownership over its poor culture that has caused top talent to apply elsewhere.

summary: 
if being immersed in a rewarding environment with positive values is important to you, then i do highly recommend working for aera. i personally have been seeking to join the company again. 

about me (as basis for my assessments and comparisons): 	
i have had the opportunity to experience much in the petroleum industry:
1.	i have worked for aera as well as other companies including a super major, one of the biggest nocs and a small independent.
2.	my practical experience includes advancing a wide range of projects (from single well recompletions to highly impactful developments) covering the entire business cycle, from exploration to field revitalization. i have worked with a great variety of reservoirs, fluid types, recovery methods, completions, etc.
3.	i had a multi-cultural upbringing and have had exposure working with people at all levels of various organization from a wealth of different backgrounds, cultural and otherwise. part of that experience includes having had the opportunity to be part of a myriad of multidisciplinary teams.

pros:
in my assessment aera offers a fantastic working experience. area’s environment and culture are superior to all others i have encountered. it is common for companies to simply advertise that their employees are the most valuable asset, what area does is actually treat their employees as their most valued asset. the work can be engaging, challenging and rewarding (it will be in part up to you and your personal drive, if you are up for it you will definitely not get bored). you will also gain valuable skills and knowledge (i improved various processes in other companies based on the experience i developed at area). the atmosphere is friendly, there is camaraderie throughout the organization and you will be treated with respect.

1.	the hr department is taken very seriously by the company (key sign of a great company). 
2.	management is properly trained to manage people.

7.	when supported by good work and an honest spirit of camaraderie, a healthy ambition to expand professionally was rewarded.
8.	work/life balance is taken seriously (i am somewhat of a workaholic so i did not always appreciate that aspect, but it was certainly there).

title: a job i don't lament being rid of...
pros: they pretended to give me a chance and acted like they acknowledged my potential for a bit.
cons:
let me start off by saying, i was an acquired employee. usually, when you inherit something from someone else, you are supposed to have a neutral view on it and accept it with open arms. when dunbar was acquired by brinks, i was one of the few, if not one of the only, who did not constantly complain out of spite. i didn't bash the new culture, the company, the employees. i went along with everything with an open mind. i thought that alone would make me stand out from the rest, nevermind my multiple years of experience in my job. without getting too personal, the acquisition came at a bad time, not that they ever come at a good one. an immediate family member of mine was battling a terminal illness, and i was the primary caregiver. my attitude and approach to work was just as vivacious as ever, and i made every effort to work remotely and be available at all times, despite caring for an immensely sick loved one. when the sale was made official, we were practically in the clear. things were looking up. no one needed to know that, because it was my personal business, but my supervisor frequently asked how my family member was doing, which i found odd because he was never one for small talk or caring any bit about my life outside of work.

as time went on, i was treated very poorly and negatively by my fellow brinks colleagues. although i had an open minded approach to working for brinks, it was obvious that the more seasoned employees there saw me as a threat. they were downright rude. still, i continued to work there. the morale amongst former dunbar employees faded and faded, until it was at an all time low. around this time, my supervisor stopped answering my calls. when i say stopped answering, i don't mean he took a long time to respond. i mean he flat-out ignored me on and off for months. this all culminated to my getting let go with no notice at all.

while a part of me will always wish that this company could have seen me for my true potential and actually valued my skill set, i realize that what happened to me is not my fault, and it is their loss, not mine. i don't miss any of it, from the poor communication to the low morale, to being ignored, to being treated so low that i dreaded coming to work every day. that being said, i don't know if i will ever forgive. there is a piece of me, a very prominent piece, that tried so very hard to appease these people, so hard that it was dominating my life, especially at a time when i should have been focusing on my loved one. i can't get that time back, but i can reflect that that's the life this company expects from you. i don't consider it coincidental at all that they found me no longer useful as soon as they found out my family member was healthy again.

as with any review i leave, my experience is here for you as a tool. take it or leave it, and make your own decision. i am sure there are people at this company who have had a great experience. read this review along with others and make your best judgment call.

title: overly structural
pros:
+ competitive salary up to recent years (75th percentile and above).
+ internal transfers/opportunities prevalent across all aspects of business (e.g. technical to commercial).
cons:
- pay structure is very rigid. middle management have no say in pay negotiations; all up to hr ultimately.
- middle management are parachuted into entirely different departments and crafts, leading to supervisors/managers that speak without technical depth and understanding.
- leadership grooming based on "who's the best at their engineering job?", which leads to managers who are good at entry level technical craft, rather than trained in leadership doctrines and people management.
- no meritocracy: when times are tough, everyone gets penalized, no incentives for those keeping the company afloat.
- next to no opportunities to negotiate compensation. due to high attrition rates, engineers have to take double roles, but salary remained frozen.

title: postdoc experience was just ok
pros:
* core mission of reducing carbon emissions and providing alternatives to carbon-based fuels is almost unbeatable as a "feel good" goal for a company or a lab

* great benefits, far better than those at university as phd student

* good pay, excellent for a postdoc

* welcoming and inclusive culture

* beautiful campus

* postdocs are supported and encouraged to be on the lookout for their next permanent opportunity
cons:
* experience is largely based on local group, and so experience can vary from team to team. my team was very good, but it could be worse for others.

* nrel uses postdocs as a form of "cheap labor." this tends to be a harmonious arrangement as postdocs get better pay and benefits than they would at a university, while still being non-competitive with private industry. the real con here, for some, is that nrel retains only a small percentage of postdocs as permanent research scientists at the end of the term. if you're looking for a postdoc -> research scientist, it is doable, but it should not be expected.

* postdocs are told that they are to focus on whatever their career goals are, and that nrel will help them get there, though the actions and policies of nrel do not reflect that goal.

* nrel uses time codes for tracking employee hours, but there are no time codes for "postdoc professional development." those of us who are established in our fields prior to arriving at nrel are given no time to nurture and cultivate an existing reputation. specifically speaking, there is no way to attend professional conferences without taking personal time off

* this leads directly into the next issue, which is pto. nrel has a good pto policy in terms of total hours given, but these hours accrue bi-weekly. since postdocs are contracted for 1 year (usually), it is indefensible that pto is only fully vested on the potential final day of employment for a postdoc. in my case, i had to use my two floating holidays to attend a professional meeting early in my employment, mid-week, which was needlessly difficult and removed two days that should have been used on actual holidays later in the year. not giving leave for professional development opportunities, and not vesting pto are two subtle ways that nrel policies can make postdocs feel unwelcome and make their lives harder than is necessary

* analysis roles, especially computer science, are not supported via the technology stack at nrel - specifically if your field relies on open-source tools built for linux, which it at nrel categorically refuses to support. my time at nrel was frustrating in that i spent more time fighting to get tools to work on a windows machine than actually using the tech to perform the analysis.

* this may have been a team thing, but i was frustrated to start on day 1 and find very low expectations for me. this turned out to be limiting. each phd is a different experience, and some of us have more experience and are more prepared to be active contributors than others. by assuming every new postdoc is essentially unable to perform on a basic level, you are actually limiting their productivity and development and de-valuing their input and ideas.

* one last point - relocation bonuses should be prorated in terms of paying them back if a postdoc leaves their term early. if the goal is truly to support postdocs finding their next endeavor, then forcing them to pay back their relocation bonuses in full, even if they are finishing their term only just before leaving, is frustrating and alienating.

title: "east is east, west is west and never the twain shall meet"
pros:
this is the story of two companies that merged a couple years ago.

employees at the franklin headquarters in fort wayne enjoy such amenities as state of the art technology; museum like exhibits; refreshment stands; a gym and walking paths; kick ball tournaments and ice cream socials. they also may participate in charity drives and list that volunteer service on resumes and social media profiles.

over at the churubusco location, formerly a company called first sales, there is a core group of employees who have worked together since before the merger. they count on each other to get the job done. if they should secretly lament on a time before the merger when their decisions did not go through the corporate conglomerate, then their comments should be seen in the context of the somewhat recent merger.
cons:
the churubusco location has none of the above amenities. due to a mistake at corporate, we became privy to email invites for the different activities at corporate. despite the fact that the 2 buildings are 30 minutes apart, churubusco employees are neither invited to participate in these activities, nor given parity. there was a lame attempt to invite us to a fall picnic. we were never sent the initial invite. we got the reminder invite instead, the week of the event. also too was the not-so-classy instruction during a company-wide live stream meeting for anyone not at hq to log out, so they could talk about the volunteer charity drive amongst themselves. when franklin boasts of these events on social media, they fail to mention the inherent unfairness in only select employee involvement. nor do they mention that the large number they list for their volunteer result is paltry compared to what volunteer efforts could have achieved if all employees were allowed to contribute.

it is true that i have not agreed with all the policies at the busco location. however, in just the last few months the franklin auditing department has asked questions regarding at least 3 subjects for which i had concerns. given the sensitive nature of these concerns, i can not list them here. that being said, not all policies that work for small companies will work once that company is merged with a larger company, especially not the policies that have the caveat: "we have always done it this way."
